prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: defendant officer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an officer's use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect does not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Officer [Name] is entitled to qualified immunity because no clearly established law forbade tasing an actively resisting suspect.**

Qualified immunity protects officers unless (1) they violated a constitutional right and (2) that right was "clearly established" when they acted. *Pearson v. Callahan*, 555 U.S. 223, 232, 236 (2009). A right is clearly established only if existing precedent places the question "beyond debate." *Ashcroft v. al-Kidd*, 563 U.S. 731, 741 (2011). The Supreme Court has repeatedly told courts not to define clearly established law "at a high level of generality." *White v. Pauly*, 580 U.S. 73, 79 (2017) (per curiam). The question is whether it was clearly established that this officer's conduct, in this situation, was unlawful. *Mullenix v. Luna*, 577 U.S. 7, 12 (2015) (per curiam). The plaintiff cannot meet that burden here.

**A. Tasing a suspect who was actively resisting was objectively reasonable under *Graham*.**

Excessive-force claims are judged by the objective reasonableness of the officer's conduct. The relevant factors are the severity of the crime, whether the suspect posed an immediate threat, and whether he was actively resisting or fleeing. *Graham v. Connor*, 490 U.S. 386, 396 (1989). The Sixth Circuit has consistently held that an officer may use a taser on a suspect who refuses to comply and physically resists. *See Rudlaff v. Gillispie*, 791 F.3d 638, 641–42 (6th Cir. 2015) (granting qualified immunity to an officer who used a taser on a suspect who was resisting arrest). *See also Hagans v. Franklin Cnty. Sheriff's Office*, 695 F.3d 505, 509 (6th Cir. 2012) (holding that using a taser on a suspect who refused to comply and resisted did not violate clearly established law). In *Goodwin ex rel. Nall v. City of Painesville*, 781 F.3d 314, 323–27 (6th Cir. 2015), this Court again analyzed taser use under the *Graham* factors. It distinguished suspects who are noncompliant or resisting from those who have been subdued.

Here, the record shows that [Plaintiff] [describe resistance: e.g., pulled away, refused repeated commands to place his hands behind his back, and struggled with officers]. Before using the taser, Officer [Name] gave [warnings/commands]. The taser was a measured response to resistance that was ongoing when he used it. It was not a response to a compliant or subdued person.

**B. No controlling precedent clearly establishes a violation on these facts.**

This Court has drawn the relevant line between resistance and its absence. Force against someone who is actively resisting is permitted. Force against someone who is subdued, handcuffed, or no longer resisting is not. *See Austin v. Redford Twp. Police Dep't*, 690 F.3d 490, 498 (6th Cir. 2012) (distinguishing force used against a suspect who was actively resisting from force used after the suspect had been subdued); *Kent v. Oakland Cnty.*, 810 F.3d 384, 391 (6th Cir. 2016) (same, and denying immunity only where a factual dispute existed over whether the suspect had stopped resisting); *Brown ex rel. Estate of Brown v. Chapman*, 814 F.3d 447, 460 (6th Cir. 2016) (same). Under these authorities, a violation depends on a suspect who has stopped resisting. Plaintiff's own conduct places him on the permitted side of that line. The precedents denying immunity involved suspects who were subdued, compliant, or no longer resisting. None of them gave Officer [Name] fair notice that tasing a suspect in Plaintiff's position was unlawful.

Plaintiff cannot rely on the general rule that gratuitous force against a non-resisting suspect is unconstitutional. That principle is stated at too high a level of generality to defeat qualified immunity. *White*, 580 U.S. at 79. The plaintiff must identify a case, or a robust consensus of cases, holding that tasing an actively resisting suspect is unlawful. He cannot do so, and the Sixth Circuit decisions above point the other way. *See Rudlaff*, 791 F.3d at 641–42; *Hagans*, 695 F.3d at 509.

**C. Resistance need not escalate to violence for a taser to be reasonable.**

This Court has not required a suspect to threaten or strike officers before a taser may be used. Active, physical noncompliance, such as refusing to give up one's hands, pulling away, or struggling, is enough to make a measured use of force reasonable and to defeat any claim of clearly established unlawfulness. *See Hagans*, 695 F.3d at 509; *Rudlaff*, 791 F.3d at 641–42. Officers must make "split-second judgments" in tense and rapidly evolving circumstances. *Graham*, 490 U.S. at 396–97. Qualified immunity protects those judgments unless every reasonable officer would have known they were unlawful. *Mullenix*, 577 U.S. at 12.

**Conclusion.** Officer [Name] tased a suspect who was actively resisting. No clearly established law told him that doing so violated the Fourth Amendment. This Court should hold that he is entitled to qualified immunity.
